nameStory: The sperm whale gets its name from the waxy substance called "spermaceti" that fills its massive head. Early whalers thought this creamy, oil-like material looked like sperm, so they dubbed it "sperm oil" and the whale became known as the sperm whale. This same valuable spermaceti made these giants prime targets during the whaling era depicted in Moby Dick.
description: The sperm whale is the largest toothed whale and the ocean's largest predator with teeth. These massive marine mammals can reach 52 feet in length, with their enormous, square-shaped heads making up a third of their total body length. Males are much larger than females and live solitary lives except during mating, while females and young travel together in protective family groups. Despite being called whales, they're actually more closely related to dolphins and other toothed whales than to baleen whales.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Enormous size with a distinctive massive, square-shaped head that looks almost box-like from the side, making up about one-third of the whale's total length

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Performs incredibly deep dives lasting up to 90 minutes, often diving straight down like a submarine rather than arcing like other whales

idTips.label: Body Features
idTips.description: Dark gray to brown skin that appears wrinkled, with a single blowhole positioned on the left front of the head rather than centered

idTips.label: Sound
idTips.description: Produces loud clicking sounds for echolocation that can sometimes be heard by nearby boats as rhythmic tapping or knocking

idTips.label: Surfacing Pattern
idTips.description: When surfacing, shows the massive square head first, then rolls forward showing a low triangular dorsal fin followed by a series of humps along the back

habitat: Sperm whales prefer deep ocean waters far from shore, typically found over underwater canyons and continental slopes where the water depth exceeds 3,000 feet. In New England waters, they're most commonly spotted over submarine canyons like Georges Bank and in the deep waters south of Cape Cod and the islands. They favor these pelagic (open ocean) areas because they can access their preferred prey of deep-sea squid through their extreme diving abilities.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing in New England's deep offshore waters as they follow seasonal feeding patterns. Best spotted during calm weather when their massive heads and distinctive spouts are visible from whale watching boats.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for potential sightings in New England waters, particularly in deep offshore areas. Their loud breathing and distinctive forward-angled spout can sometimes be detected before the whale is seen.
seasonality.fall: May still be present in deeper offshore waters before beginning seasonal migrations. Calmer seas make this an excellent time for spotting their distinctive square heads when they surface.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters as they typically migrate to warmer regions for breeding. Any winter sightings would be exceptional and likely involve individuals following deep-water prey.

funFact: Sperm whales produce the loudest sounds of any animal on Earth - their echolocation clicks can reach 236 decibels underwater, loud enough that they could theoretically stun or even kill nearby prey with sound alone, making them living sonic weapons of the deep.
confusionNotes: The massive square head is unmistakable - no other whale has this box-like profile. If you can see the head clearly, you've definitely found a sperm whale. Other large whales like humpbacks and fin whales have streamlined, pointed heads that look completely different.
contextualKnowledge: These are the whales of Moby Dick fame, and the whaling industry that once dominated New England was largely built around hunting sperm whales for their valuable spermaceti oil and ambergris. The term "spermaceti" has nothing to do with reproduction - it's simply what early whalers called the waxy substance in the whale's head because of its appearance.
compareHints: Sperm whales are the only living members of their genus, making them unique among whales. Their closest relatives are the much smaller pygmy and dwarf sperm whales, but these are rarely seen and only reach 12 feet maximum compared to the sperm whale's 52-foot length. The massive square head and deep-diving behavior immediately distinguish sperm whales from all other large whales in New England waters.
